clean_story:
"Liquid color. Permanent marks.
The word ink comes from the Latin incus, meaning ‘to stain,’ as it leaves a lasting trace on surfaces.

Most see ink as a simple tool for writing, yet its true nature is a suspension of pigments or dyes in a liquid that dries into a solid film. Like a river carrying sediment to form new land, ink deposits color particles onto paper, fabric, or skin, binding them as the solvent evaporates. The oldest known ink, India ink, dates back to 2500 BCE in China, made from soot and animal glue—its carbon particles resist fading even after millennia. Modern ballpoint pens use a oil-based ink that dries instantly, unlike fountain pen ink, which relies on water evaporation. Tattoo ink suspends pigments in a carrier fluid, designed to resist the immune system’s attempt to flush it out, leaving designs permanent under the skin.

Three related subjects are pigment chemistry, calligraphy tools and printing history."
